lesson.title: The Bridge: Splitting One Big Collision Domain in Two
lesson.summary: A bridge is a device that connects two network segments and decides, frame by frame, whether traffic needs to cross from one side to the other. It was the conceptual ancestor of the modern switch and the first device to bring MAC address intelligence to Ethernet forwarding.
lesson.body:
A bridge is a device that connects two separate network segments and makes an intelligent decision about which frames need to cross between them. Where a hub blindly repeats every signal to every port with no understanding of what it is repeating, a bridge actually reads the destination MAC address in each Ethernet frame and uses that information to decide whether the frame belongs only on the segment where it originated or needs to be passed through to the other side.

The bridge accomplishes this by keeping an internal table that associates MAC addresses with the segment, effectively the port, through which each address can be reached. When a frame arrives, the bridge checks whether the destination address lives on the same segment the frame came from. If it does, the bridge filters the frame, meaning it deliberately does not forward it, because forwarding would be pointless: the destination device already saw the frame directly on its own shared segment. If the destination lives on a different segment, the bridge forwards the frame across to that segment. If the bridge does not yet know where the destination lives, or the frame is a broadcast, it floods the frame out to every segment except the one it arrived on, erring on the side of delivery.

This filter or forward decision is the single biggest improvement a bridge offers over a hub, and it directly benefits collision domains. Recall that every device on a hub shares one collision domain and competes for the same airtime. A bridge splits a large shared network into two smaller collision domains, one per segment, and only forwards traffic across the boundary when it actually needs to cross. Local traffic on one side stays local and never consumes bandwidth on the other side at all.

Picture an office building with two wings, each wing wired as its own hub based segment, and a bridge connecting the two hubs together. When a computer in the east wing sends a file to a printer also in the east wing, the bridge sees the frame, checks its table, notices the printer's address belongs to the same segment the frame arrived from, and filters it: the frame never crosses into the west wing, so west wing devices experience zero additional traffic from that print job. But when someone in the east wing emails a large attachment to a colleague's computer in the west wing, the bridge recognizes the destination belongs to the other segment and forwards the frame across, exactly the moment its filtering intelligence is supposed to yield to forwarding.

The bridge's core idea, examine the destination address, consult a table, and forward only where necessary, is precisely what an Ethernet switch does today. In fact, a modern switch is best understood as a bridge with many ports instead of just two, with each individual device getting its own dedicated segment rather than sharing one with several others, and with the address lookup logic implemented directly in fast hardware rather than software. How that address table gets built and kept up to date, entirely automatically and without any administrator configuration, is the subject of the next chapter.
